evidence: TaskManagementService takes UserRepository, ProjectRepository and TaskRepository (domain interfaces) through its constructor and only calls save/findById/findByProject on them: it coordinates storage but does not implement it.
completeTask hands the state change to the domain function markDone(...) and then saves the result, which is typical use-case orchestration.

addTask checks the input (requireText for title, the typeof check on description, new Date(...) with a NaN check on dueDate) and confirms the project and assignee exist. This is boundary validation and checking that referenced entities exist, both of which belong in the application layer.
The file has no HTTP, routing, serialization or database code.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/application/services.ts fits the application layer. TaskManagementService coordinates use cases: it creates users and projects, adds, assigns, lists and completes tasks. It checks that referenced entities exist, works through repository interfaces defined in the domain layer, and hands the domain transition to markDone. It has no persistence code (no SQL or storage access), no transport code (no HTTP, request or response handling) and no framework code. The input checks (requireText, the string-to-Date parsing of dueDate, the type check on description) clean up untyped input at the use-case boundary, which is normal application-layer work. The ID generation (randomUUID) and the default values when building a Task could arguably sit in domain factories, which makes the domain model somewhat thin. But these are borderline design choices, not a clear case of one layer doing another layer's job. No ADR prose was given that says otherwise.
